source.title: Towards the Scalable Evaluation of Cooperativeness in Language Models
source.authors: Alan Chan; Maxime Riché; Jesse Clifton

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how cooperative choices vary with model size, but does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit scaling laws to loss, test extrapolation, or estimate compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its scaling results concern a different outcome from the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling work and reports cooperative-action trends across model sizes. These are not measurements of cross-entropy loss or downstream-task performance: the authors do not define the choices as correct answers or a performance score. The reported cooperative-choice trends are recorded as findings about the claim's subject under fits_no_version, not as tests of V1–V7. The cited scaling-law results are not the paper's own results.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates cooperative action choices of GPT-3 and UnifiedQA on game-theoretic scenarios across model sizes. It does not measure pretraining loss, fit power laws, test extrapolation or compute-optimal allocation, or score downstream task performance. The choices are not framed as correct answers, so the size trends do not bear on V6. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only in the introduction. The record's relation 'tests' contradicts its own T6 tranche; corrected to cites_only.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors' main conclusion is that generating and verifying scenarios with specific game-theoretic structure was very difficult for both crowdworkers and an LM; the prisoner's-dilemma false-positive rate reached 0.85. Secondarily, larger instruct-tuned GPT-3 models tended toward cooperative-seeming choices, while other models showed flat trends. The authors present the results as suggestive and a snapshot of particular prompts and models.
record.recipe_differences: Measures action choices on cooperation-game evaluations across model sizes, rather than fitting held-out loss scaling laws or testing compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports no overall significant behavior differences attributable to time-horizon descriptions. In the largest instruct GPT-3 model, roleplay prompts produced significant deviations from the no-roleplay baseline; the game-theorist prompt reduced equal dictator-game offers and prisoner’s-dilemma cooperation.

fits_no_version.finding: In the GPT-3 instruct series, larger models more often chose proportionate punishment, equal dictator splits and rejection of stingy ultimatum offers. Non-instruct GPT-3 and UnifiedQA showed flat trends with size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Instruction tuning, not size alone, drives size-related increases in conventionally fair or cooperative choices in simple economic games.

record.problems: The paper reports that synthetic scenarios and their evaluation were often poor quality, including high rejection rates and a false-positive rate of 0.85 for prisoner’s-dilemma judgments. Scaling figures provide plotted values, while the text mainly gives qualitative trend descriptions; exact model sizes and many exact results are not stated. The authors caution that results reflect a particular moment and particular prompts.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for time-horizon or roleplay results: these report prompt sensitivity of action choices, not additional scaling-law or loss findings. No individual model-size values were extracted from the plots.

untested.parts: All: no held-out loss is measured.
All: no fits and no extrapolation.
All: no power-law fits in other regimes.
All: action-choice probabilities are not downstream performance scores, and no predictability from scale or loss is assessed.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation field ('tests') was inconsistent with its tranche (T6) and its own gate note; corrected to cites_only. The model sizes on the plots are ordinal only, and no exact values are given in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from smaller-run fits.
Loss-minimizing parameter and token allocations at fixed compute.
Effects of architecture details on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream-task performance as a score predicted by scale or pretraining loss; the study measures action choices, not task performance.
Dependence of fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices.
